36.title: The tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
36.hook: one language, one tower, and a scattering into many peoples
36.howItsDone: Jews read the Babel story each autumn in the Torah portion Noach, and teachers often pair it with the midrash about the fallen brick to ask what a community values.

segments.voice: Last week ended with brit: the covenant with every living thing, and the bow in the cloud. Your line was a promise to everything. Did you keep your small promise? A new week. Day thirty-six.

It opens with a sentence like the start of a fairy tale. In the old JPS translation: "And the whole earth was of one language and of one speech." People travel east and settle on a plain. And someone has an idea. Come, let's make bricks and bake them hard. Let's build a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and make a name for ourselves, so we won't be scattered over the face of the earth. So they build. And then comes a line that's almost funny. The tower is meant to reach heaven, and God has to come down to see it. Today: the tallest building in Genesis, and why it never got finished.
screen: `ONE LANGUAGE, ONE SPEECH.` → `LET US MAKE A NAME.` → `GOD COMES DOWN TO SEE IT.`

segments.voice: God confuses their language, so they can't understand each other, and scatters them over the earth. The building stops. The place is called Babel, the Torah says, because there God confused, in Hebrew balal, the language of all the earth. Babel is also the Hebrew name for Babylon, the great city. So the name itself is a pun. Here's the honest part. The Torah never says exactly what the builders did wrong. They don't kill anyone. They don't break a commandment. The sources are quiet, and so readers have filled the silence in different ways. Some point to the words make us a name: a project to glorify themselves. Some point to lest we be scattered: God had told Noah's children to fill the earth, and they huddled together instead. And one old midrash tells a haunting story. The tower grew so tall that carrying a brick to the top took a year. When a worker fell to his death, nobody stopped. When a brick fell, they sat down and wept, because it would take a year to replace. The building had become worth more than the builders. Some later commentators, reading one language and one speech, heard something else: a world where everyone was made to say the very same words. On that reading, the scattering isn't only a punishment. It's a rescue. Many peoples, many languages, many ways of saying the same good morning. The world after Babel is noisier, and it's more human.
screen: `BALAL — TO CONFUSE.` · `THE TORAH NEVER NAMES THE SIN.` · `THE BRICK MATTERED MORE.` · `SCATTERING AS A RESCUE.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of a language spoken by someone near you: a coworker, a neighbor, the family that runs the corner shop, a grandparent. Picture that person's face. Do you know how to say hello in their language? Good morning? Thank you? If you do, say it silently to yourself. If you don't, sit with the wish to learn it. No tower. Just one word across the gap. The bell holds the time.
The tower of Babel. A city built to make a name, left unfinished, and a scattering into many peoples and many languages.
Your line: many tongues. Today, learn one greeting in another language, and if you can, use it with someone who speaks it. Day thirty-six.

37.title: Go forth (Genesis 12:1–3)
37.hook: Abram is told to leave land, birthplace and father's house for a place not yet named
37.howItsDone: Lech Lecha is the name of the weekly Torah portion that begins with this call, read in synagogues each autumn, and its opening words are often quoted for anyone setting out on a move or a new stage of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the tower of Babel, a city built to make a name, and a scattering into many languages. Your line was many tongues. Did you learn a greeting? Day thirty-seven.

Imagine a man of seventy-five, settled, with land and flocks and family around him, in a city called Haran. His father's household is there. Everything he knows is there. And one day God speaks to him, and in the old JPS translation it sounds like this: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto the land that I will show thee." That's it. No map. No address. Not even the name of the place. Just: go, and I'll show you when you get there. Anyone who has ever moved for a job, left home for college, or packed up after a breakup knows a little of that feeling. Today's words are the two that start it all.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE, AND SETTLED.` → `GET THEE OUT.` → `A LAND NOT YET NAMED.`

segments.voice: Lech lecha. Lech means go. Lecha means, literally, to you, or for you. So the plainest translation is just go, but the Hebrew has that strange little extra: go for yourself. Rashi, the medieval commentator, reads it as go for your own good: this journey is for you. And later Hasidic teachers read it more boldly: go to yourself. The outward journey is also an inward one. Now look at the order: your country, your birthplace, your father's house. If you were actually leaving, you'd walk out of your father's door first, then the town, then the country. The Torah lists it the other way, from the widest to the closest. Commentators notice that each step cuts nearer to the heart. The hardest thing to leave comes last. Then the promise: I will make of thee a great nation, and bless thee, and make thy name great; and, the verse ends, "in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed." Remember Babel yesterday? The builders said, let us make us a name. Here God says, I will make thy name great. The same thing they tried to grab is given as a gift, to someone who walks away from everything to receive it. And Abram goes. The Torah doesn't tell us how he felt. The rabbis count this among the ten tests of Abraham. The phrase lech lecha appears only once more in the Torah, and it's the last and hardest test. For now, he simply goes before he knows.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the paths you walk every day without deciding to: the same street to work, the same aisle in the store, the same chair, the same first app you open. Pick one. Picture taking a different way, just once. What might you see that you've never noticed? Stay with the small unease of not knowing exactly what's around the corner. If you pray, you can ask for courage for one small step. The bell holds the time.
Lech lecha. Go, for yourself, or go to yourself. The call that starts Abram's journey, and the name of this Torah portion.
Your line: go before you know. Today, take a different route somewhere, a street, a store, a way home, and see what the new path shows you. Day thirty-seven.

38.title: Abram breaks the idols (Genesis Rabbah 38)
38.hook: a rabbinic story: young Abram smashes his father's idols and blames the biggest one
38.howItsDone: Jewish schools and families often tell the story of Abram and the idols when the Torah portion Lech Lecha is read, making clear that it comes from the midrash Genesis Rabbah rather than the Torah itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was lech lecha: go, for yourself, to a land not yet named. Your line was go before you know. Which new route did you take? Day thirty-eight.

Here's a story many Jewish kids know by heart. Abram's father, Terah, makes idols and sells them. One day he leaves young Abram to mind the shop. A customer comes in, and Abram asks how old he is. Fifty, sixty. And you'd bow down to something made yesterday? The man leaves, embarrassed. Then a woman brings a plate of fine flour as an offering for the gods. Abram picks up a stick, smashes every idol in the shop, and puts the stick in the hands of the biggest one. His father comes home. What happened here? Abram says: a woman brought flour, the gods started fighting over who'd eat first, and the big one got up and smashed the rest. His father snaps: are you mocking me? They can't do anything! And Abram says: let your ears hear what your mouth just said.
screen: `TERAH'S IDOL SHOP.` → `A STICK IN THE BIG ONE'S HANDS.` → `LET YOUR EARS HEAR YOUR MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise. That story isn't in the Torah. Not a word of it. It comes from Genesis Rabbah, a collection of rabbinic teachings on Genesis put together in the land of Israel many centuries after the Torah. It's a midrash. Midrash comes from the Hebrew root darash: to seek, to search, to dig into. It's the way the rabbis read the Torah: by asking questions of it and filling its silences. And the Torah is silent about a lot. Yesterday God said to Abram, go. But why Abram? Genesis never says. It doesn't tell us a single thing about his childhood, or what he believed, or why God chose him. Midrash answers: because he questioned. He looked at a statue and asked whether it could really do anything. Another midrash in the same book has a lovely picture. A man is traveling and sees a great house on fire. He wonders: can it be that this house has no owner? And the owner looks out and says, I am the owner. So Abram looked at the world, beautiful and burning, and asked who was responsible, and God answered. The rabbis were clear about something important here. The Talmud says a verse never loses its plain meaning. Midrash doesn't replace what the text says; it sits beside it, asking. That's why Jews can love a midrash and also know it's a midrash. The tradition itself teaches people to question the statue, even a statue made of stories.
screen: `NOT IN THE TORAH AT ALL.` · `DARASH — TO SEEK, TO DIG.` · `WHY ABRAM? GENESIS IS SILENT.` · `THE HOUSE ON FIRE.` · then, large: `QUESTION THE STATUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you just assume. A thing you've never really questioned: that you're bad at math, that a certain neighbor doesn't like you, that you need your phone the moment you wake up, that things have to be done the way they've always been done. Pick one. Look at it the way Abram looked at the statue. Can it really do what you think it does? Where did it come from? You don't have to smash anything. Just ask. The bell holds the time.
Midrash. From darash, to seek. The rabbis' way of asking questions of the Torah and filling its silences with stories.
Your line: question the statue. Today, take the one assumption you found, and ask it honestly whether it's true. Day thirty-eight.

39.title: Abram and Sarai in Egypt (Genesis 12:10–20)
39.hook: famine, fear and a half-truth that nearly costs everything; the Torah doesn't hide its heroes' faults
39.howItsDone: Jews read this episode in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and commentaries such as Nachmanides are studied alongside it, including his criticism of Abram's choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was midrash, and a boy who smashed his father's idols. Your line was question the statue. What assumption did you question? Day thirty-nine.

Abram has just arrived in the land God promised him. And the first thing that happens there is a famine. So he keeps going, south, down to Egypt, where there's grain. At the border, he turns to his wife. You're beautiful, he tells Sarai. When the Egyptians see you, they'll kill me and keep you. Say you're my sister, so that it goes well with me because of you. And that's exactly what happens. Pharaoh's officials see her, praise her to Pharaoh, and she's taken into the palace. Abram, the brother, is rewarded with sheep and cattle and donkeys and camels. The man who was just promised a great name is standing in Egypt, getting rich, while his wife is in another man's house. Today: the Torah's first hero, afraid.
screen: `FAMINE IN THE PROMISED LAND.` → `SAY YOU'RE MY SISTER.` → `SARAI IN PHARAOH'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Then God strikes Pharaoh's household with plagues, and Pharaoh figures it out. He calls Abram in, and in the old JPS translation he says: "What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?" Think about who's asking. Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is the one with the moral question. Abram doesn't answer. Pharaoh gives Sarai back and sends them away. Now, was it a lie? Later in Genesis, in a very similar scene, Abraham says Sarah really is his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not his mother. So, a half-truth. But a half-truth told to save himself, while she paid the price. The rabbis did not look away from this. Nachmanides, the great thirteenth-century commentator, says it plainly: Abram sinned. He put his righteous wife at risk out of fear, and he should have trusted God to protect them both. Others defend him: the danger was real, and he had no good choices. Jewish tradition keeps both voices in the room. And notice what the Torah never tells us: what Sarai said, or felt. Her voice is silent here. Nachmanides also noticed a pattern. Famine sends a family down to Egypt; Pharaoh's house is struck with plagues; they leave with wealth. That's the whole book of Exodus in a few verses. The rabbis had a saying for it: what happens to the parents is a sign for the children. The first hero stumbled, and the Torah wrote it down.
screen: `WHAT IS THIS THOU HAST DONE?` · `A HALF-TRUTH, AND SHE PAID.` · `NACHMANIDES: ABRAM SINNED.` · `A SIGN FOR THE CHILDREN.` · then, large: `HEROES STUMBLE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days for one small untruth. Not a big betrayal. The ordinary kind: I'm fine. I didn't see your message. I'm almost there. Find one, and notice what it protected. Was it fear? Comfort? Someone's feelings? Then notice who paid for it, even a little. Don't punish yourself. Just admit it, to yourself, honestly. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Abram and Sarai in Egypt. A famine, a fear, and a half-truth, told in full by a Torah that doesn't hide its heroes' faults.

segments.voice: Your line: heroes stumble too. Today, when you catch yourself shading the truth out of fear, stop and say the plain thing instead. Day thirty-nine.

40.title: Abram lets Lot choose (Genesis 13)
40.hook: to keep the peace, the elder lets his nephew take first pick of the land
40.howItsDone: Jews read this story in the Torah portion Lech Lecha; its words "for we are brethren" and Hillel's teaching about loving and pursuing peace are often quoted when family members or neighbors settle a dispute.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abram and Sarai in Egypt, a famine, a fear and a half-truth. Your line was heroes stumble too. Did you catch yourself shading the truth? Day forty.

Abram comes back from Egypt rich: cattle, silver and gold. His nephew Lot, who came with him, has his own flocks and herds and tents. And now there's a problem every family with a shared inheritance knows. There isn't room for both of them. The land can't feed all those animals in one place, and the herdsmen start to fight. Abram's shepherds against Lot's. Shoving at the wells. Arguments over grass. You can feel it heading toward something worse. And Abram is the elder. God promised this land to him, not to Lot. He could simply tell his nephew where to go. Instead, he does something that surprises everyone who has ever split a pizza, a bedroom or a family house. Today: who picks first.
screen: `TOO MANY SHEEP, NOT ENOUGH GRASS.` → `THE HERDSMEN FIGHT.` → `THE ELDER COULD DECIDE.`

segments.voice: Abram says to Lot, in the old JPS translation: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we are brethren." In Hebrew, anashim achim: we are men who are brothers. Then he points at the whole land. Is it not all before you? If you go left, I'll go right. If you go right, I'll go left. You choose first. So Lot lifts up his eyes and looks. He sees the plain of the Jordan, well watered everywhere, green like the garden of God, and he takes it, and moves his tents toward a city called Sodom. The Torah adds one quiet, ominous line: the men of Sodom were very wicked. Hold on to that; we'll come back there. Now notice the eyes. Lot lifted his eyes and chose what looked best. Right after Lot leaves, God speaks to Abram: lift up your eyes, look north and south and east and west. All the land you see, I give to you and your children. Walk through it. What Abram let go of came back to him as a gift, and bigger. The rabbis added their own note. One midrash says the fight started because Lot's shepherds let their animals graze in other people's fields, while Abram's kept theirs muzzled. The later sages turned the whole scene into a value: Hillel taught, be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing it. Sometimes that means being the one who says: you choose first.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the small daily contests in your life. Who gets the good chair. Which show to watch. Where to eat. Whose turn it is. Who speaks first in the meeting. Pick one that's coming up today. Picture yourself turning to the other person and saying, you choose. Notice what that feels like in your body: tight, or loose? Stay with it. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart. The bell holds the time.
Abram lets Lot choose. The elder, who had every right to pick, gives the first choice away to keep the peace between brothers.
Your line: you choose first. Today, in one small contest, let the other person choose first, and mean it. Day forty.

41.title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
41.hook: childless and old, Abram is told to look up and count the stars
41.howItsDone: Jews read this vision in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and the verse "he believed in the LORD; and He counted it to him for righteousness" is often studied as the Torah's first picture of emunah, faith as trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abram lets Lot choose, for we are brethren. Your line was you choose first. Who did you let choose? Day forty-one.

Abram is old now, and God speaks to him in a vision. In the old JPS translation: "Fear not, Abram, I am thy shield, thy reward shall be exceeding great." And Abram, who so far in the story has mostly just obeyed, answers back. What will you give me? I'm going childless. The heir of my house is my steward, Eliezer of Damascus. You've given me no children. It's the voice of anyone who has been promised something for years and is starting to stop believing it: a job, a family, a recovery, a change. What good is a great reward, if the thing I actually want never comes? And God doesn't argue. God takes him outside.
screen: `FEAR NOT, ABRAM.` → `WHAT WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `GOD TAKES HIM OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Outside, under the whole night sky, God says: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." And then: "So shall thy seed be." Picture it. No city lights, no haze. On a clear desert night, the sky is thick with stars, too many to count. That's the point. The task is impossible. It isn't a math problem. It's a way of making an old man tip his head back and look up. The rabbis had fun with this. The Talmud imagines Abram saying: I've read my own stars, and they say I won't have a son. And God answers: step outside your astrology. You are not bound by the stars. Another midrash says God lifted Abram up above the stars, so that he looked down on them. Either way, the sky that seemed to say no is turned into a yes. Then comes one of the most important sentences in Genesis: "And he believed in the LORD; and He counted it to him for righteousness." The word for believed shares a root with amen: to be firm, to lean your weight on something. And the word for righteousness is tzedakah, from tzedek, the word we met with Noah. In the English, count appears twice: Abram is told to count the stars, and, in the most common reading, God counts his trust as righteousness. He couldn't finish counting. He didn't have to. He looked up, and he leaned on the promise.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. If you can, close your eyes and picture a night sky, the darkest you've ever seen: at a campsite, a beach, a field far from town. Let the stars fill in, one by one, until there are too many. Now bring to mind one promise you're still waiting on, or one hope that feels old. Don't solve it. Just hold it under that sky. If you pray, you can lean on it there. The bell holds the time.
Count the stars. An impossible task that makes an old man look up, and the first time the Torah says Abram believed.
Your line: look up and count. Tonight, go outside, look at the sky for one full minute, and start counting, knowing you won't finish. Day forty-one.

42.title: Hagar names God (Genesis 16)
42.hook: a runaway servant meets an angel at a spring and calls God "the God who sees me"
42.howItsDone: Jews read Hagar's story in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and her name for God, El Roi, the God who sees me, is often taught as a reminder to notice people who are overlooked.

segments.voice: Yesterday: count the stars, if you're able, and Abram believed. Your line was look up and count. Did you get outside and look? Day forty-two.

Ten years in the land, and still no child. So Sarai does something that was a known custom in that world and is hard to hear in ours. She gives her Egyptian servant, Hagar, to Abram, hoping for a child through her. Hagar conceives. And the household cracks. Hagar looks down on Sarai. Sarai treats her harshly. And Hagar, pregnant and alone, runs away into the desert, on the road back toward Egypt. She stops at a spring of water in the wilderness. And there, the Torah says, an angel of God finds her. Think of the least important person in a big, rich household: the foreign servant, the one nobody asks. She is the first person in the Torah an angel comes to.
screen: `TEN YEARS, NO CHILD.` → `HAGAR RUNS INTO THE DESERT.` → `AN ANGEL FINDS HER.`

segments.voice: The angel speaks first, and the first word is her name. In the old JPS translation: "Hagar, Sarai's handmaid, whence camest thou? and whither goest thou?" Here's a detail worth noticing. In this whole chapter, Sarai and Abram never once say her name. They call her my handmaid, thy maid. The angel is the first to call her Hagar. Then comes the hard part. The angel tells her to go back to her mistress. Readers have struggled with that for centuries, and some of the great commentators, like Nachmanides, said openly that Sarai did wrong in afflicting her, and Abram did wrong in allowing it. But the angel also gives her a promise of her own: a son, and many descendants. Call him Ishmael, the angel says, which means God hears, because God has heard your affliction. And then Hagar does something no one else in the Torah does. She gives God a name. She calls God El Roi. "Thou art a God of seeing," in the JPS wording: the God who sees me. The spring gets a name too: Beer-lahai-roi, the well of the Living One who sees me. Hold that together. A servant nobody named is named by an angel. A woman nobody listened to is told that God heard her. And the one nobody saw names God as the one who sees. Her son's name means God hears. Her name for God means God sees. In one chapter, the Torah's least powerful person gets both.
screen: `THE ANGEL SAYS HER NAME.` · `A HARD COMMAND, A PROMISE.` · `ISHMAEL — GOD HEARS.` · `EL ROI — GOD WHO SEES ME.` · then, large: `THOU ART A GOD OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the people you pass every day without really seeing them. The person who cleans the office. The cashier. The bus driver. The quiet kid in the group chat. The neighbor you only know by their dog. Pick one. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Do you know their name? If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, just see them, fully, for a minute. The bell holds the time.
El Roi. The God who sees me: Hagar's name for God. That's the sixth week: Babel, lech lecha, midrash, Egypt, Lot's choice, the stars, and El Roi.
Your line: you are seen. Today, notice someone who usually goes unseen, and let them know it: their name, a thank-you, a real look. Day forty-two.
